subject: Medicine
summary: Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is a breach of the gastric or duodenal mucosa caused mainly by H. pylori infection or NSAID use. It presents with epigastric pain and can lead to bleeding or perforation if untreated.

sections.p: A peptic ulcer is a mucosal defect ≥5 mm that extends through the muscularis mucosa into the submucosa, confirmed by endoscopy or radiography.
b: Endoscopy is gold‑standard; shows ulcer size, location, stigmata of recent hemorrhage.
Rapid urease test or stool antigen confirms H. pylori.

t.b: Does the patient have an ulcer and what are its high‑risk features? Positive finding confirms diagnosis and guides therapy.

t.a: H. pylori test (urease, stool antigen, breath test)
t.b: Is H. pylori present? Positive result directs eradication therapy; negative suggests NSAID or other cause.

sections.p: Severity is staged by ulcer size, depth, and presence of complications (bleeding, perforation, obstruction). The Forrest classification grades bleeding risk.
b: Forrest Ia–IIb = high risk, need urgent endoscopic therapy.
Forrest III = low risk, can be managed medically.

sections.p: Identify the primary driver to target treatment.
b: H. pylori infection – most common worldwide.
Regular NSAID or aspirin use – especially in elderly.
Smoking, alcohol, stress – aggravating factors.

sections.p: Typical pain is epigastric, described as burning, often relieved by food (duodenal) or worsened by food (gastric).
b: Nighttime pain waking the patient.
Occult or overt GI bleeding (melena, hematemesis).
Weight loss if chronic obstruction develops.

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions.
b: Endoscopy for diagnosis and risk stratification.
H. pylori testing to decide eradication.

t.b: Is there anemia from chronic bleeding? Low hemoglobin suggests occult bleed, prompting endoscopic evaluation.
Is there hypergastrinemia suggesting Zollinger‑Ellison? Markedly elevated levels warrant further imaging.

sections.p: Recognize features that need urgent care.
b: Sudden severe abdominal pain → perforation.
Hematemesis, melena, or drop in hemoglobin → bleeding.
Persistent vomiting, weight loss → obstruction.

sections.p: Treat the cause, protect the mucosa, and monitor healing.
b: Eradicate H. pylori with a proton‑pump inhibitor (PPI) plus clarithromycin and amoxicillin/metronidazole.
Stop NSAIDs; switch to acetaminophen or COX‑2 selective agents if needed.
PPI therapy (high‑dose) promotes ulcer healing and reduces re‑bleed risk.
Avoid bismuth in patients with renal failure; avoid steroids without gastro‑protection.
Repeat endoscopy 6–8 weeks after therapy if high‑risk ulcer or persistent symptoms.
Test for H. pylori eradication (urease or stool antigen).
Educate on avoiding NSAIDs, smoking cessation, and moderate alcohol.
Gastritis – inflammation without a true mucosal breach.
Gastro‑esophageal reflux disease – heartburn predominates.
Functional dyspepsia – pain without endoscopic lesion.
Negative H. pylori test after recent antibiotics or PPIs may be false; repeat after washout.
Mild anemia may be missed if only hemoglobin is checked; consider iron studies.

whenToSeekHelp: Vomiting blood or black tarry stools (bleeding)
Rapid drop in blood pressure or fainting

faq.q: Why are NSAIDs a major risk for peptic ulcers?
faq.a: They inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, reducing mucus and bicarbonate protection of the gastric lining.

faq.q: Can a peptic ulcer heal without medication?
faq.a: Small, uncomplicated ulcers may heal, but untreated H. pylori or ongoing NSAID use leads to recurrence or complications.

faq.q: Is stress alone enough to cause an ulcer?
faq.a: Stress can worsen symptoms but is not a primary cause without H. pylori or NSAID exposure.

exam: Describe the diagnostic steps for a patient with suspected duodenal ulcer and explain the role of H. pylori testing.
List the first‑line treatment regimen for H. pylori‑positive peptic ulcer disease and justify each drug class.
Identify three red‑flag symptoms that require urgent endoscopic evaluation.
